findings.source_passage: He might have despised himself, for he had certainly taken her under false pretences. I don't mean that he had traded on his phantom millions
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'He might have despised himself'
findings.why_it_matters: This paragraph contains the interpretively critical phrase 'phantom millions' and establishes the precise nature of Gatsby's deception — not financial fraud but existential misrepresentation. Critical readings of the novel depend on this distinction; its erasure collapses a morally nuanced passage into a flat summary.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this paragraph substantially, at minimum preserving 'He might have despised himself, for he had certainly taken her under false pretences. I don't mean that he had traded on his phantom millions, but he had deliberately given Daisy a sense of security.' The 'phantom millions' phrase and the false-pretences framing are non-negotiable.

findings.source_passage: "In any case," he said, "it was just personal." What could you make of that, except to suspect some intensity in his conception of the affair that couldn't be measured?
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Suddenly he came out with a curious remark'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves the line 'it was just personal' but drops Nick's interpretive gloss entirely. That gloss is the moment Nick registers Gatsby's incomprehensible romantic absolutism; without it, the cryptic remark merely hangs in the air rather than pointing toward Gatsby's transcendent self-conception.
findings.suggested_fix: Add Nick's follow-up observation: 'What could you make of that, except to suspect some intensity in his conception of the affair that couldn't be measured?' immediately after the reported line.

findings.source_passage: fresh faces drifted here and there like rose petals blown by the sad horns around the floor
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'For Daisy was young and her artificial world'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reduces this richly imagistic paragraph to one compressed sentence, losing its most distinctive images: 'grey tea hour,' 'rooms that throbbed incessantly with this low, sweet fever,' and especially the 'rose petals blown by the sad horns' simile — one of the novel's most evocative prose-poetic moments.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at least the 'rose petals' simile and the 'grey tea hour / rooms that throbbed' image; these are the sentences that establish the decadent beauty of Daisy's world and motivate her capitulation to Tom's 'wholesome bulkiness.'

findings.source_passage: He left feeling that if he had searched harder, he might have found her—that he was leaving her behind.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'He left feeling that if he had searched harder'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence crystallizes the Louisville episode's emotional logic — Gatsby's irrational guilt over a departure he could not have prevented. The draft moves directly to the train imagery without this psychological anchor, making the departure feel merely melancholy rather than the specific self-torturing delusion that characterizes Gatsby.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'He left feeling that if he had searched harder, he might have found her—that he was leaving her behind' before the description of the hot day-coach.

findings.source_passage: The shadow of a tree fell abruptly across the dew and ghostly birds began to sing among the blue leaves.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'It was dawn now on Long Island'
findings.why_it_matters: This dawn image contributes to the chapter's elegiac atmosphere and provides a specific, memorably precise sensory register at the pivot from night confession to morning farewell; its absence slightly flattens the tonal transition.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the single sentence about the tree's shadow and the ghostly birds to maintain the dawn atmosphere before Gatsby's defensive speech about Daisy.

findings.source_passage: with an effort he got up and walked to the rear window and leaned with his face pressed against it
findings.source_locator: Wilson's speech to Michaelis about God, near end of Wilson vigil section
findings.why_it_matters: The physical staging of Wilson pressing his face to the glass — juxtaposed with his unknowing contemplation of the Eckleburg billboard — is dramatically essential to the scene's power; the draft reports the speech but strips the body language that makes the Eckleburg revelation visceral.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Wilson rising with effort, walking to the rear window, and pressing his face against it before his speech, so the Eckleburg revelation lands with its intended shock.

summary: The draft commits one high-severity signature loss (the 'phantom millions' / false-pretences paragraph, which carries critical and interpretive weight essential to understanding Gatsby's deception) and three medium-severity losses (Nick's gloss on 'it was just personal,' the rose-petals-and-sad-horns imagery from the Daisy twilight-world paragraph, and the Louisville 'leaving her behind' sentence), triggering a regenerate verdict.
